'''Theodore Cohen''' (May 11, 1929 – December 13, 2017) was an American [[organic chemistry|organic chemist]] and chemistry professor at [[University of Pittsburgh]].<ref name=utimes/><ref name=cen>{{cite news |title=Theodore Cohen |url=https://cen.acs.org/articles/96/i17/Theodore-Cohen.html |access-date=June 23, 2018 |work=Chemical & Engineering News}}</ref><ref name=pg>{{cite news |title=Obituary: Theodore 'Ted' Cohen / A quirky renowned chemist |url=https://www.post-gazette.com/news/obituaries/2017/12/26/Obituary-Theodore-Ted-Cohen-A-quirky-renowned-chemist-dead-88/stories/201712240131 |access-date=June 23, 2018 |work=[[Pittsburgh Post-Gazette]] |language=en}}</ref><ref name=pitt>{{cite news |title=Obituary: Professor Theodore Cohen transformed chemistry department|url=https://pittnews.com/article/126573/news/life/obituary-pitt-professor-transformed-chemistry-department/ |access-date=June 23, 2018 |work=[[The Pitt News]] |date=January 21, 2018}}</ref> He is known for his research on [[organic chemistry]],<ref name=utimes/> and particularly on [[organosulfur compounds]],<ref name=pg/><ref name=crucible/> on [[organometallic chemistry]],<ref name=pitt/><ref name=crucible/> and on the synthesis of [[phenol]]s.<ref name=marks>{{cite news|url=https://www.utimes.pitt.edu/archives/?p=5584|title=Chemistry prof Cohen marks 50 years at Pitt|date=October 26, 2006|newspaper=University Times|publisher=University of Pittsburgh}}</ref>

==Education and career==
Cohen was born in Boston, the son of a [[furrier]] from England, and was the first in his family with a college education.<ref name=pg/> He graduated from [[Tufts University]] in 1951 with a degree in chemistry.<ref name=utimes/><ref name=cen/> He was guided towards science instead of medicine in a chance encounter with [[Isaac Asimov]] while working a summer job as a waiter,<ref name=pg/> and completed his Ph.D. in chemistry at the [[University of Southern California]] in 1955,<ref name=utimes/><ref name=cen/> helping to support his graduate studies by working as an extra in the movies of [[Katharine Hepburn]] and [[Spencer Tracy]].<ref name=pg/> His doctoral research, supervised by [[Jerome A. Berson]], concerned the synthesis of [[alkaloid]]s found in [[ipecac]], and the chemical properties of [[pyridine]]s.<ref name=crucible/>

After postdoctoral research as a [[Fulbright scholar]] at the [[University of Glasgow]], working with [[Derek Barton]],<ref name=marks/> he joined the University of Pittsburgh chemistry faculty in 1956,<ref name=utimes/> and became one of the first professors at the university to bring in federal grant money for his research.<ref name=utimes/><ref name=pitt/> He retired as a [[professor emeritus]] in 1999, but continued to do research in his laboratory, often working 80-hour weeks.<ref name=utimes/><ref name=crucible/>

At the University of Pittsburgh, he was the [[doctoral advisor]] to over 40 students.<ref name=pitt/>

==Recognition==
He was the 2009 winner of the Pittsburgh Award of the Pittsburgh section of the [[American Chemical Society]].<ref name=pitt/><ref name=crucible>{{cite journal|url=http://www.pittsburghacs.org/wp-content/uploads/2011/10/cruc_06aug09.pdf|journal=The Crucible|publisher=ACS Pittsburgh Section|volume=94|issue=10|date=August 2009|title=The Pittsburgh Section ACS Announces 2009 Award Winners|page=2}}</ref>

==Personal life==
[[File:Isaac.Asimov01.jpg|thumb|upright|[[Isaac Asimov]] in the 1950s, when he befriended Cohen while on vacation]]
Cohen worked at a holiday camp in Massachusetts while he was a student at Tufts.  While waiting tables, he courted Pearl Silverman, a bookish woman from New York.  The biochemist and author, [[Isaac Asimov]], also vacationed there and became friends with Cohen.  Observing the romance, Asimov wrote songs about it for the camp show, "Poor Ted's in bed. He's lonely but well read";  the couple were later married and went on to have two children, Bret and Rima.{{r|pg}}

He died of [[chronic lymphocytic leukemia]] at a hospice in the [[Squirrel Hill]] neighborhood of Pittsburgh on December 13, 2017.<ref name=pg/>
